notes.key_messages: Where a qualitative test is split into a number of steps, then observations should be recorded for each step in the order the steps are carried out.
notes.general_comments: The majority of candidates successfully completed both questions and there was no evidence that candidates were short of time. All Centres submitted Supervisors’ results with the candidates’ scripts. Not all Centres used the specified reagents but used a substitute. If Centres are concerned that one of the specified reagents will not be available for the examination then they should contact CIE at the earliest opportunity to seek advice.
notes.1a: Almost all candidates correctly recorded effervescence.
notes.1d: Some candidates recorded only one colour, rather than the colour before and after the addition.
notes.1e: Most candidates recorded their results from all four experiments; a small minority incorrectly calculated one or more temperature difference. A relatively common error was to record temperatures to differing numbers of decimal places.
notes.1f: Almost all candidates drew a bar chart as instructed, with only a very few attempting to draw a line graph. There were few errors in drawing bars to the correct heights.
notes.1gi: While many correct responses were seen, there were many incorrect reaction types stated, such as precipitation, displacement or redox. Some candidates gave two answers; this almost invariably meant that one of their answers was wrong.
notes.1gii: Better performing candidates could relate the effervescence to the production of carbon dioxide from the reaction between a carbonate and an acid. Some candidates thought that the gas was hydrogen and that the white solid D must be a metal.
notes.1h: Most candidates were able to correctly identify the experiment with the largest temperature change.
notes.1hi: While many candidates recognised that the pH increased or that it was a neutralisation reaction, only a small fraction of those continued their answer to state that G was a base.
notes.1j: A number of candidates did not realise that because the reaction would be over, the temperature would return to room temperature. Some candidates thought the temperature would continue to increase at the same rate and so predicted temperatures which should have been identified as implausible.
notes.1k: The most common error was for candidates to think that a larger volume of acid meant a faster reaction and so a larger temperature change.
notes.2a: Most candidates gave an acceptable description of the appearance of solid H . Descriptions of appearance should include colour.
notes.2b: The recorded observations suggest that many candidates did not heat gently at first as required. Relatively few candidates noted the initial formation of a liquid or the condensation in the upper reaches of the test-tube.
notes.2c: Some candidates incorrectly reported that solid H was insoluble.
notes.2d: Better performing candidates gave an observation for each instruction. Others just gave one set of observations for all three instructions together. Although the gas produced was ammonia, few commented on the smell and some reported the production of an acidic gas.
notes.2e: Despite the fact that the precipitate formed in this test is the same precipitate as the one formed in (d) candidates often reported different colours from those reported in (d) .
notes.2f: Some candidates reported positive halide ion tests. Negative tests are helpful in identifying ions in a salt.
notes.2g: Most candidates reported the formation of a precipitate, but some reported results such as the precipitate re-dissolving or being coloured.
notes.2h: As many candidates missed the formation of condensation, they did not state that solid H was hydrated. The identification of ammonia gas being given off was more common, although some mistakenly stated that solid H itself was alkaline.
notes.2hi: This was well answered by those candidates who correctly reported no reaction in (f) , although some mixed up halogens with halide ions.
notes.2j: Candidates found identifying the three ions in solid H challenging. Candidates should include the oxidation state when identifying iron ions, such as iron (III) or iron (II).
